title: Seeing Red, Thinking Bad: Color Bias in VLMs
hook: Render the same sentence with the positive words in green and a vision-language model reads it more positively. The text didn't change — only its styling did.
key_points: VLMs increasingly read text that arrives as an image — screenshots, documents, slides.
Stealth Visual Prompts alter visual styling (color, contrast) while leaving semantic content intact.
Coloring positive words green consistently shifts sentiment predictions in the positive direction.
Under that shift, models often fail to properly account for negative words in the same text.
Lower text–background contrast increases reliance on visually salient cues and produces more VQA errors.
The authors correlate the effect with color-induced changes in the vision encoder's latent representations.
content_html: Vision-language models are ending up in decision-making pipelines — recruitment support, recommendations — and a lot of what they read arrives as pixels rather than tokens: screenshots, PDFs, slides. That raises a question nobody asks of a plain text model. Does it matter what the text looks like?
extra_html:
Stealth Visual Prompts

The authors introduce Stealth Visual Prompts: perturbations that change the visual styling of rendered text — colour, contrast — while preserving its semantic content exactly. Then they systematically vary the styling of individual words and measure what the model concludes.

Colouring positive words green consistently shifted sentiment predictions in the positive direction. The revealing part is the follow-on effect: under that shift, models often failed to properly account for negative words present in the same text. Separately, reducing text–background contrast increased reliance on visually salient cues and produced more incorrect visual question answering outputs.

Where it comes from

Probing the vision encoder, the authors find the behaviour correlates with colour-induced changes in its latent representations — the styling isn't being ignored and then recovered at the language stage; it perturbs the representation the language model reasons over.

The practical warning is direct: if a VLM screens rendered documents, whoever formats those documents holds a channel of influence that never appears in the text.

related.title: Look Light, Think Heavy: The Limits of Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
related.hook: Chain-of-thought should make models think harder. For vision-language tasks this study finds it's no free lunch — it can hurt perception, and models keep talking while they stop looking.

related.title: Where VLM Localization Signal Actually Hides in Editing Pipelines
related.hook: VLMs are great at pointing to objects on their own — but bolt one onto a diffusion image editor and that skill seems to vanish. It didn't leave, it just hid somewhere editing pipelines don't look.

related.title: An Exam for Active Observers
related.hook: Human vision is a loop — look, form a hypothesis, look again. A new benchmark for that loop leaves frontier MLLMs scoring single digits, while humans average 96%.

flashcards.prompt: What is a Stealth Visual Prompt?
flashcards.back_html: A change to the visual styling of text rendered as an image — colour, contrast — that preserves the semantic content while measurably shifting how a VLM interprets it.

flashcards.prompt: What happened when positive words were coloured green?

choices.text: Sentiment predictions shifted positive, and models often failed to account for negative words present
Models refused to answer, flagging the input as manipulated
Sentiment predictions were unchanged but confidence dropped

flashcards.explanation_html: Colouring positive words green consistently pushed sentiment in the positive direction, with the model under-weighting the negative words in the same text.

flashcards.prompt: What effect did reducing text–background contrast have?

choices.text: It increased reliance on visually salient cues and produced more incorrect VQA outputs
It made the model fall back to pure text reasoning and improved accuracy
It had no measurable effect once the text was still legible

flashcards.explanation_html: Lower contrast pushed the model toward whatever was visually salient, leading to more incorrect answers on visual question answering.
